Tutor’s top tips
Whilst it would be possible to calculate the capital allowances by doing a revised
computation, not all of the figures for that computation (such as the brought forward balance
on the main pool) were provided in the question. Therefore, it would be necessary to do
significantly more workings (to establish the missing figures) if this approach were taken. It is
therefore easier to simply correct the mistakes you are aware of via short workings as shown.
Tutorial note
1  |  The issue of preference shares is not a trading expense and therefore the associated
legal fees are not an allowable deduction.
2  |  Legal fees are treated in the same way as the loan they relate to. The loan was for
trading purposes, therefore the fees are a deductible trading expense.
3  |  Legal fees relating to a lease are only deductible if it is therenewal of a short (50 years
or less) lease. The lease here is over 50 years long and as such the legal fees are not an
allowable deduction for tax purposes and need to be added back.
4  |  Legal fees in relation to the registration of trademarks relate to the trade, and are
therefore tax deductible.
5  |  Since it is only the life of the lease which was incorrect in the original calculation, this
can be corrected by simply multiplying the figure given by the 12 years used originally
and dividing by the correct figure of 15 years. It is not necessary to try to recalculate
the deduction from scratch, and this would prove very difficult as the figure for the
premium paid was not provided in the question.
6  |  Cars 1 and 2 have CO2 emissions between 1 and 50 grams per kilometre, and qualify
for writing down allowances at the rate of 18%. No adjustment is therefore required.
7  |  Car 3 has CO2 emissions over 50 grams per kilometre, and therefore only qualifies for
writing down allowances at the rate of 6%. The extra 12% (18% – 6%) that had been
calculated originally therefore needs to be deducted from the total capital allowances.
8  |  Car 4 has zero emissions, and therefore qualifies for 100% first year allowance. In the
absence of any other information, assume that cars purchased are new (not second-
hand). Therefore, an additional allowance of 82% (100% – 18%) needs to be included.
9  |  The scrapping of the computer equipment is a disposal for capital allowances purposes.
The company should therefore have received a 100% balancing allowance rather than
a writing down allowance at the rate of 18%. The 82/18 adjustment represents the
additional 82% (100% – 18%) of the brought forward TWDV which can be deducted.
This could also have been calculated by comparing the correct balancing allowance
(£1,512/18% = £8,400) with the amount that had previously been deducted (£1,512).
10 As the repairs were carried out in order to make the warehouse usable, they are treated
as capital in nature and are therefore disallowed. However, structures and buildings
allowance (SBA) at 3% can be claimed on these costs since they were incurred after
1 April 2020 (the relevant date for TX exams). SBA can only be claimed from the date
the property was brought into use, i.e. the day it was first let out – 1 July 2025.
11 Property and interest income must be dealt with on an accruals basis, therefore an
adjustment is required for the rent due and the correct loan interest accrual.
(b) Quarterly instalment payments
Tutor’s top tips
Being able to determine when corporation tax is payable is a common examination
requirement, and it is important to learn the rules about which companies must pay by
quarterly instalments and the exceptions from that system, which are relevant here.
•  |  Large companies have to make quarterly instalment payments in respect of their
corporation tax liability. A large company is one with augmented profits
exceeding £1,500,000, adjusted for short accounting periods and associated
companies.
•  |  However, a company is not required to make quarterly instalment payments in
the first year that it is large.
Therefore, E-Commerce plc will not have been required to make instalment
payments for the year ended 31 March 2026 as it was not a large company in
the year ended 31 March 2025.
This is because the augmented profits of £1,360,000 were less than £1,500,000.
•  |  For the year ended 31 March 2027, this exception will not apply. Therefore,
E-Commerce plc will have to make quarterly instalment payments as its
augmented profits will exceed £1,500,000.

Part (a) was not particularly difficult, but the information was presented in a different format
to previous questions of this nature. However, candidates would have benefited from
knowing the pro forma layout.
The requirement was generally reasonably well answered and there were a few highly
satisfactory answers. The deduction for the lease premium caused the most problems, with
many candidates not appreciating that there was no need to recalculate the amount taxed
on the landlord – thereby spending quite a bit of time unnecessarily.

title: Q261 · STRETCHED LTD (ADAPTED)
scenario:
This scenario relates to two requirements.
Stretched Ltd has always prepared its accounts to 31 December, but has decided to change
its accounting reference date to 31 March. The company’s results for the 15-month period
ended 31 March 2026 are as follows:
1  |  The tax adjusted trading profit is £642,500. This figure is before taking account of
capital allowances.
2  |  Until January 2026 the company has never been entitled to capital allowances as all
assets were leased. On 15 January 2026 the company bought office equipment for
£50,000, and a car with CO2 emissions of 42 grams per kilometre for £7,500.
3  |  There is a property business profit of £45,000 for the 15-month period ended 31 March
2026.
4  |  On 15 April 2025 the company disposed of some investments, and this resulted in a
chargeable gain of £44,000. On 8 February 2026 the company made a further disposal,
and this resulted in a capital loss of £6,700.
5  |  Dividend income of £30,000 was received on 10 September 2025.
6  |  A qualifying charitable donation of £5,000 was made on 31 March 2026.
As at 1 January 2025 Stretched Ltd had unused trading losses of £330,000, and unused capital
losses of £3,000. Stretched will make a claim to relieve these losses as soon as possible where
necessary.
In the year ended 31 December 2024 the company had taxable total profits of £Nil and no
dividend income.
Stretched Ltd has no associated companies.

date of 31 March instead of 31 December.  (2 marks)

Key answer tips
This question requires the calculation of a company's taxable total profits for a three-month
accounting period. It encompasses adjustments to trading profit, capital allowances, and the
computation of a chargeable gain.
You should begin by adjusting the given accounting loss for non-allowable expenses. Make

the short accounting period on the different allowances.

incidental costs of acquisition and disposal. Apply indexation allowance to both the original
cost and any enhancement expenditure up to December 2017.

Examiner’s report
The corporation tax question was very well answered, with many candidates scoring high
marks. The question required candidates to calculate Cop Ltd’s trading loss and taxable total
profits for the three-month period 1 October to 31 December.
As for the income tax question, there were various ways of approaching this question. Again,
the easiest one was to have a main computation working out the trading loss, with this then
extended to include the chargeable gain and qualifying charitable donation to arrive at a
figure for taxable total profits. Capital allowances and the chargeable gain both warranted
separate workings.
In regard to the main computation, there were two issues which sometimes caused
problems:
•  |  Candidates were instructed to indicate by the use of zero (0) any items which did not
require adjustment. There were in fact five items of expenditure where no adjustment
was required (because they were allowable), representing a total of 2.5 marks. A
number of candidates did not do as instructed and therefore would not have gained
these very easy 2.5 marks even if the remainder of their workings were correct.
Remember it is important to read and follow the instructions given in the requirement.
•  |  With this type of answer containing both additions and deductions, candidates should
be very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions
shown clearly as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion. Those candidates who
did not show the deductions clearly invariably had problems when it came to showing
totals with negative entries, and it was sometimes difficult for markers to determine
whether a figure was a plus or a minus.
One other point to bear in mind is that candidates should answer a question in the order in
which information is provided. The information was provided in the order (1) donations, (2)
legal and professional fees, (3) promotional costs and (4) annual party. So, adjustments
should follow the same sequence. If this approach is followed, it allows markers the
opportunity to sometimes award a mark where an obvious mistake has been made.
Capital allowances
The fact that the accounting period was only three months long meant care had to be taken
with the capital allowances working:
•  |  The £1,000,000 annual investment allowance expenditure limit was £1,000,000 × 3/12
= £250,000.
•  |  There was no restriction in regard to first-year allowances.
•  |  The 18% and 6% writing down allowances were both restricted by 3/12ths.
Despite these complications, quite a number of candidates correctly calculated the capital
allowances figure for 5 marks, with many achieving 4 or 4.5 marks.
The main problem was with the car in the special rate pool which was bought (for £57,000)
and sold (for £50,000) during the accounting period. Despite this being the only asset in the
special rate pool, there was not a balancing adjustment, but, instead, a writing down
allowance calculated as normal.
Chargeable gain
The chargeable gain was probably the most difficult aspect of this question, especially as two
separate indexation allowance workings were necessary.
•  |  The incidental costs had to be picked up from the disallowance of legal and
professional fees. This figure was then deducted from the disposal proceeds, so was
not relevant when it came to the indexation allowance calculations.
•  |  One surprising mistake was sometimes the indexation allowances were calculated, but
then only those figures deducted and not the cost and enhancement expenditure
figures on which the indexation allowances were based.
Candidates should particularly note that the annual exempt amount is NOT relevant to
corporation tax.

title: Q263 · WRETCHED LTD (ADAPTED)
scenario:
This scenario relates to three requirements.
Wretched Ltd started trading on 1 August 2025, preparing its first accounts for the eight-
month period ended 31 March 2026.
Wretched Ltd is incorporated in the United Kingdom, but its three directors are all non-
resident in the United Kingdom. Board meetings are always held overseas.
The following information is available:
Trading loss
The trading loss based on the draft accounts for the eight-month period ended 31 March
2026 is £141,200. This figure is before making any adjustments required for:
1  |  Advertising expenditure of £7,990 incurred during April 2025. This expenditure has not
been deducted in arriving at the trading loss for the eight-month period ended
31 March 2026 of £141,200.
2  |  The premium which was paid to acquire a leasehold office building on a ten-year lease.
3  |  Capital allowances.
Premium paid to acquire a leasehold office building
On 1 August 2025, Wretched Ltd paid a premium to acquire a leasehold office building on a
ten-year lease. The amount of premium taxed on the landlord as income was £34,440. The
office building was used for business purposes by Wretched Ltd throughout the eight-month
period ended 31 March 2026.
Plant and machinery
On 1 August 2025, Wretched Ltd purchased three new laptop computers at a discounted cost
of £520 per laptop. The original price of each laptop was £950, but they were sold at the
discounted price because they were ex-display.
Wretched Ltd also purchased three second-hand cars on 1 August 2025. Details are:

£
Car 1  |  8,300  |  0 grams per kilometre
Car 2  |  12,300  |  50 grams per kilometre
Car 3  |  18,800  |  65 grams per kilometre
Property income
Wretched Ltd lets out a warehouse which is surplus to requirements. The warehouse was let
out from 1 August to 31 October 2025 at a rent of £1,400 per month. The tenant left on
31 October 2025, and the warehouse was not re-let before 31 March 2026.
During the eight-month period ended 31 March 2026, Wretched Ltd spent £2,100 on
advertising for tenants.
Due to a serious flood, Wretched Ltd spent £5,900 on repairs during January 2026. The
damage was not covered by insurance.
Loss on the disposal of shares
On 20 March 2026, Wretched Ltd sold its entire 1% shareholding of £1 ordinary shares in
Worthless plc for £21,400. Wretched Ltd had purchased these shares on 5 August 2025 for
£26,200.
Other information
Wretched Ltd does not have any associated companies. Wretched Ltd will continue to trade
for the foreseeable future.
requirement:
Required:
(a) State, giving reasons, whether Wretched Ltd is resident or not resident in the United
Kingdom for corporation tax purposes.  (1 mark)
(b) Assuming that Wretched Ltd is resident in the United Kingdom, calculate the
company’s trading loss, property income loss and capital loss for the eight-month
period ended 31 March 2026.
Note: You should assume that the company claims the maximum available capital
allowances.   (11 marks)
(c) Explain how Wretched Ltd will be able to relieve its trading loss, property income
loss and capital loss for the eight-month period ended 31 March 2026.   (3 marks)
(Total: 15 marks)

Key answer tips
The first mark available was in relation to company residence and was straightforward. You
should be prepared to be tested on this topic.
The calculation of three separate losses was required: a trading loss, a property loss and a
capital loss.
The capital allowances computation was the largest section of the trading loss calculation.
Knowledge of the different treatment of cars based on the level of emissions was required
here. This is regularly tested in the examination. Also, remember to time apportion
allowances, except for the first year allowance, for a short accounting period.
The calculation of property income is tested regularly. This should have been straightforward

Examiner’s report
For part (a), candidates were required to state whether the company was resident or not
resident in the UK for corporation tax purposes. This requirement resulted in a very surprising
amount of incorrect answers, with at least half the candidates deciding that the company
was not resident because of its central management and control being exercised overseas.
Part (b) required a calculation of the company’s trading loss, property business loss and
capital loss. As regards the trading loss, this involved pre-trading expenditure, a deduction
for a lease premium and capital allowances. This section was generally very well answered,
although there were a couple of consistent problems. Firstly, it was often not appreciated
that a second-hand car does not qualify for the 100% first year allowance. [Part of the
examiner’s report has been removed as it relates to a topic which is no longer examinable.]
For part (c), candidates were required to explain how the company would have been able to
relieve its trading loss, property business loss and capital loss. Provided candidates
appreciated that it was the company’s first period of trading, this section was then well
answered. However, candidates who overlooked this basic fact spent a lot of time discussing
all the various (irrelevant) loss reliefs, with a few candidates discussing the income tax relief
for a loss incurred in the early years of a trade.

CRUMBLE LTD
Key answer tips
This question on corporation tax losses starts with a requirement to calculate the amount of
the corporation tax loss and then a calculation of the taxable total profits without any relief
for the loss.
The remaining parts require consideration of when a loss carry back claim should be made
and how much corporation tax will be repaid if the carry back claim is made.
The highlighted words in part (c) are key phrases that markers are looking for.

–––––––
(b) Taxable total profits for the nine-month period ended 31 December 2025
£

–––––––

–––––––
Tutorial note
A security deposit, less the cost of making good any damage, is returned to the tenant on the
cessation of a letting. It is therefore initially not treated as income.
(c) (i) Claim
A claim must be made by 31 December 2027 (within two years of the end of the
period ended 31 December 2025, the loss-making period).
(ii) Repayment of corporation tax
The loss carried back is (£177,850 – £15,370) = £162,480
This is less than Crumble Ltd’s taxable total profits of £466,300 for the year
ended 31 March 2025 (but results in a TTP figure above £250,000, meaning the
main rate of tax still applies), so the corporation tax repayable is (£162,480 ×
25%) = £40,620.
Tutorial note
As the year end 31 March 2025 all falls in FY2024, and even after loss relief the taxable total
profits exceed £250,000 (£466,300 – £162,480 = £303,820) the corporation tax was at 25%.
In order to carry the loss back to y/e 31 March 2025 a current period claim must be made first
against total profits of the period ended 31 December 2025 (as calculated in requirement (b)).

Examiner’s report
The corporation tax question was generally reasonably well answered, although few
candidates scored high marks.
Crumble Ltd had made a trading loss for the nine-month period ended 31 December 2025,
but had other income for this period and had taxable total profits for the year ended
31 March 2025.
Requirement (a) – 7 marks
This requirement was not answered as well as may be expected, given it was a fairly
straightforward loss adjustment scenario:
•  |  Several candidates failed to score very easy marks by not indicating the non-adjustable
items with a zero, despite being instructed to do so. There were seven such items, so
this basic mistake could have cost a potential 3.5 marks.
•  |  The deduction for interest payable was ignored by many candidates, despite the
requirement specifically referring to this note in the question scenario. On the other
hand, few of those candidates who did include an adjustment computed the correct
figure. The interest figure included in the summarised income statement was £8,750.
This figure related to the period 1 March to 30 September 2025. A further three
months of interest therefore had to be added (£5,000 × 3/6 = £2,500), making a total
interest deduction of £8,750 + £2,500 = £11,250.
•  |  Some candidates attempted to rewrite the summarised statement of profit or loss in
order to get to the tax adjusted trading loss. Apart from ignoring the instruction to
commence with the operating loss figure, this approach was much more complicated;
making it difficult to gain all the marks.
•  |  The requirement specifically instructed candidates to ignore the information given in
respect of the property business income and the chargeable gain, yet several
candidates did not comply with this and wasted quite a bit of their time.
•  |  The best approach to this requirement was a single-column list commencing with the
operating loss as a negative figure and listing the items referred to in the relevant
notes. Provided the interest was also included as a negative, it was then just a case of
using the SUM function to get to the tax adjusted trading loss. The simplicity of this
approach is that the same layout can be used regardless of whether a profit or a loss
is involved.
Requirement (b) – 4 marks
There were many good answers for this requirement, with quite a few candidates achieving
full marks.
Candidates had to take account of the property business income, the chargeable gain and
the qualifying charitable donation, and were instructed in the requirement to only take
account of this information. However, a number of candidates included the trading loss or
even the taxable total profits for the previous period. Again, in doing so they would have
certainly wasted time.
The most common problem was with the chargeable gain where figures were provided for
both the original cost and for the indexed cost. Some candidates invariably deducted both
figures, and this resulted in a capital loss rather than a chargeable gain. Once again, this
shows why it is important to read the question and requirements as carefully as possible.
Requirement (c)(i) – 1 mark
The correct answer was by 31 December 2027, which is two years from the end of the loss-
making period.
There were few correct answers for this requirement, with answers spread across a wide
range of alternative dates.
Requirement (c)(ii) – 3 marks
Although there were some perfect answers to this requirement, overall, it was not
particularly well answered.
Many candidates ignored the current period loss relief claim, with others calculating the
revised corporation tax liability for the year ended 31 March 2025 rather than the
corporation tax refund.
The answer was simply the trading loss (calculated in part (a)), less the current year total
profits (the property business profits and chargeable gain from part (b)) at 25%. Even if this
approach was used, however, many candidates included the current year qualifying
charitable donation, thereby missing out on a half mark.
Quite a few candidates just stated that the corporation tax originally paid would be fully
refunded. Although a mark was given for this, candidates needed to go further to gain any
additional marks. For example, if a candidate’s own-figure trading loss was greater than total
profits in the year ended 31 March 2025 (so that a full refund was in fact the correct answer),
a further half mark was given for an appropriate explanation.

Examiner’s report
The corporation tax question was generally quite well answered, although (somewhat
surprisingly) the capital allowances working in part (b) caused problems. Candidates often
ended up with a reasonably correct answer to part (c)(i), where loss relief was claimed, but
spent a lot of time on irrelevant workings in reaching that point.
One common problem seen in part (b) was the inability to deal with negatives. The
requirement was to calculate Mooncake Ltd's tax adjusted trading loss, commencing with
the operating loss figure of £93,820. This meant that the adjustments for non-allowable
expenditure reduced the amount of loss, but the loss was increased by capital allowances.
As shown in the suggested solution, the easiest approach was to start with £93,820 as a
negative figure, show non-allowable expenditure as positive figures and then include capital
allowances as another negative. This is then consistent with a profit adjustment question
commencing with a profit, avoiding the loss of some easy marks if negatives and positives
are confused. The total can then be obtained using the SUM function on the spreadsheet.
Some candidates showed all figures as positive and then tried to calculate the total within
the cell on the lines of – A1+A2+A3-A4. It is also very easy to make mistakes using this
approach.
The only aspect requiring a separate working was one for capital allowances.
Requirement (a)
Although many candidates easily picked up the [three] available marks, many instead wrote
at length about available loss reliefs.
The fact that this requirement is just for [3] marks, together with the use of ‘state’ should be
a very good indication that only a short set of answers is required. This is why it is important
to make use of the model answers since candidates’ answers should, ideally, not be any
longer than those.
Candidates who mentioned loss of personal allowances or annual exempt amounts had,
worryingly, confused income and corporation taxes.
Requirement (b)
When answering this type of question, candidates are advised to answer in the same order
as information is presented. So here, the first item was depreciation, and that, therefore,
should have been the first adjustment. This approach makes it easier for markers to follow a
candidate’s answer, and there is less scope for missing out any of the adjustments.
As can be seen from the suggested solution, the capital allowances working was fairly
straightforward, involving just a main pool. There were three disposal figures to deduct from
the brought forward written down value, with an 18% writing down allowance calculated on
the remaining balance. The only reason for providing the cost figures was so that (where
relevant) proceeds could be restricted to original cost. However, many candidates included
the cost figures as additions, and there were then various permutations involving balancing
adjustments. Again, this is why question practice is so important.
It should also be noted that none of the other information (property business loss and profit
on disposal of shares) was relevant to this part of the question since the requirement was
just to calculate the tax adjusted trading loss.
Requirement (c)(i)
With only losses for the year ended 31 March 2026, there was obviously no income. However,
this should have been indicated by the use of zeros (0). There was no chargeable gain because
the indexation allowance of £6,700 exceeded the gain of £3,700. This did not create a loss,
and there was no need to utilise the capital loss brought forward from the year ended
31 March 2025. These were both common mistakes made by candidates.
Another common mistake was to carry back the property business loss. Many candidates
assumed that the qualifying charitable donations for the year ended 31 March 2025 were
wasted despite the trading loss being considerably less than income. The suggested solution
shows how it is much easier to lay out this type of answer using a two-column approach with
one column for each year. Although most candidates did reasonably well in this part, there
were not many perfect answers.
Requirement (c)(ii)
Although marks were awarded based on what candidates had done in part (c)(i), the need to
carry out an overall review and see what was left appeared to be challenging for many
candidates. The correct answer was that there was an unused capital loss from the year
ended 31 March 2025, and a property business loss from the year ended 31 March 2026. For
full marks, it was also necessary to show that the trading loss had been fully utilised, and that
the unused qualifying charitable donations from the year ended 31 March 2026 were wasted.
So four points for a half-mark each, and what should have been a very short answer.
There were very few perfect answers, with many candidates picking up just one or two half-
marks and wasting time on unnecessary detailed workings.
The use of ‘calculate’ in the requirement should have indicated that no explanation was
necessary.
Note: The examiner’s report has been edited regarding elements of the question that have
been edited due to changes in the tax legislation.

MUSIC PLC (ADAPTED)
Key answer tips
In this question there are ten marks for written explanations of the gains group and
associated company rules. It is important to state the basic rule and then apply to the facts
of the question. Be careful with the overseas company, which is included but unable to enjoy
the benefits of gains group status.
The highlighted words in the answer are key phrases that markers are looking for.
(a) Capital gains group
•  |  Companies form a capital gains group if at each level in the group structure there
is a 75% shareholding, provided the parent company has an effective interest of
more than 50%.
•  |  Alto Ltd, Bass Ltd, Cello Ltd, Echo Inc and Flute Ltd are all 75% subsidiaries, and
Music plc has an effective interest of 60% (80% × 75%) in Flute Ltd. All of these
companies therefore form a capital gains group.
•  |  However, Bass Ltd and Cello Ltd will only be included in respect of assets
acquired or disposed of whilst they were members of the group.
•  |  Drum Ltd and Gong Ltd are not included as Drum Ltd is not a 75% subsidiary,
and Music plc’s effective interest in Gong Ltd is only 48% (80% × 75% × 80%).
•  |  Although Echo Inc is included in the definition of the capital gains group,
companies that are resident overseas are not able to take advantage of the
provisions applicable to a capital gains group.
(b) Associated companies
•  |  Alto Ltd, Bass Ltd, Cello Ltd, Echo Inc, Flute Ltd and Gong Ltd are all under the
common control of Music plc, and are therefore associated companies.
•  |  Companies associated for part of the accounting period, such as Bass Ltd and
Cello Ltd, count as associated companies for the whole of the period.
•  |  For these purposes, it does not matter where a company is resident. Echo Inc is
therefore included despite being resident overseas.
•  |  Drum Ltd is not included as an associated company since Music plc’s effective
interest in this company is only 45%.

(d) Bank loan
Under the loan relationship rules, the cost of loans used for non-trade purposes are
deductible from interest income. If the loan was used to acquire a property which was
to be rented out (i.e. a non-trade purpose), the interest would not be deducted from
trading income, nor property business income (as for individuals), but from the
company’s interest income.
Legal fees
Legal fees incurred in relation to the purchase of a capital asset are not deductible
from the company’s trading profits. They will be deductible in the chargeable gain
computation when the building is ultimately sold.
Rent receivable
The rent receivable from letting the property to a tenant will be included on an accruals
basis, net of any allowable deductions, in taxable total profits as property income.

The corporation tax question involved three unconnected limited companies, Ash Ltd, Beech Ltd
and Cedar Ltd.
Part (a)(i) for 2 marks was to identify Ash Ltd’s accounting periods throughout the period
1 December 2023 (incorporation) to 31 March 2026 (the end of the first twelve-month set of

If asked to identify a company’s accounting periods throughout a given period candidates
should make sure that all relevant periods are stated. It does not create a good impression if
there are gaps between the accounting periods stated by a candidate, or if a stated period
ends before it has started.
Part (a)(ii) required candidates to explain Ash Ltd’s residence status throughout the same

applicable to individuals. If a limited company is incorporated in the UK, then nothing else is
relevant. So, as regards the majority of Ash Ltd’s director/shareholders moving overseas,
candidates should just have stated that this did not have any impact on the company’s
residence status.

31 January 2026. The requirement for 6 marks was to calculate the company’s corporation
tax liability for this year. Various adjustments were required, but there were no capital
allowances. This section was very well answered.
When making adjustments to a trading profit, candidates need to be very careful that
adjustments are correctly added and not deducted.
Cedar Ltd had made a chargeable gain on the disposal of a shareholding on 28 December
2025. For the year ended 31 March 2026, the company made a trading loss. Cedar Ltd was a
100% subsidiary company of Timber Ltd, and for the year ended 31 March 2026, Timber Ltd
had made a trading loss and also a capital loss.
Part (c) for 5 marks required a calculation of Cedar Ltd’s taxable total profits for the year
ended 31 March 2026. This was on the basis that all available claims and elections were
made. This section was again well answered. When calculating chargeable gains for a
corporate share disposal carefully check the dates that have been given. There was a rights
issue which had taken place in the month of purchase, so there was no need to index prior
to adding the new shares into the share pool.

title: Q269 · LONG LTD AND ROAD LTD (ADAPTED)
scenario:
(a) This scenario relates to one requirement.
Long Ltd owns 100% of the ordinary share capital of Road Ltd. Long Ltd and Road Ltd
are both trading companies.
Long Ltd’s shareholding in Road Ltd was acquired on 15 January 2025 when that
company was incorporated. Long Ltd has prepared accounts for the year ended
31 March 2026, whilst Road Ltd has prepared accounts for the period 1 January 2026
(when the company started trading) to 31 March 2026.
The following information is available:
Long Ltd
1  |  The operating profit for the year ended 31 March 2026 is £384,400. Depreciation
of £43,050, amortisation of £5,000 and leasing costs of £3,600 have been
deducted in arriving at this figure. The amortisation relates to a premium which
was paid on 1 August 2021 to acquire a leasehold office building on a 20-year
lease. The amount of premium taxed on the landlord as income was £68,200.
The office building was used for business purposes by Long Ltd throughout the
year ended 31 March 2026. The leasing costs relate to a car with a CO2 emission
rate of 82 grams per kilometre, which was leased from 1 April 2025.
2  |  On 1 April 2025, the tax written down value of the plant and machinery main
pool was £44,800. On 10 June 2025, Long Ltd purchased a new lorry for £47,840
and a new car for £15,700. The car has a CO2 emission rate of 42 grams per
kilometre. The car is used by the managing director of Long Ltd, and 40% of the
mileage is for private journeys.
3  |  On 1 February 2026, Long Ltd disposed of a 2% shareholding in an unconnected
company. The disposal resulted in a capital loss of £21,300.
Road Ltd
1  |  The operating loss for the three-month period ended 31 March 2026 is £26,100.
Donations of £2,800 have been deducted in arriving at this figure. The donations
consist of political donations of £400 and qualifying charitable donations of
£2,400.
2  |  On 3 October 2025, Road Ltd purchased a car for £11,600. The car has zero CO2
emissions.
3  |  For the three-month period ended 31 March 2026, loan interest receivable was
£4,300. The loan was made for non-trading purposes.
4  |  On 18 March 2026, Road Ltd disposed of a 1% shareholding in an unrelated
company. The disposal resulted in a chargeable gain of £29,800. This figure is
after taking account of indexation.
Other information
Road Ltd is not expected to be profitable for the foreseeable future, and Long Ltd and
Road Ltd claim maximum possible group relief where group relief is available.
requirement:
Required:
On the assumption that any available reliefs are claimed as soon as possible,
calculate the corporation tax liability of Long Ltd for the year ended 31 March 2026,
and of Road Ltd for the three-month period ended 31 March 2026.  (12 marks)
(b) This scenario relates to one requirement.
Road Ltd’s recently appointed bookkeeper understands that the company must report
PAYE information to HM Revenue & Customs in real time. However, the bookkeeper
does not know how PAYE real time reporting works in practice, having previously only
produced payroll manually.
Road Ltd pays its employees at the end of each calendar month, with some employees
receiving taxable benefits. Road Ltd has chosen not to tax the benefits through the
payroll system.
Required:
Explain how and when Road Ltd will have to report real time PAYE information to
HM Revenue & Customs, and state what forms, if any, will have to be provided to
employees or submitted to HM Revenue & Customs following the end of the tax
year.    (3 marks)
(Total: 15 marks)

LONG LTD AND ROAD LTD (ADAPTED)  |  Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor
Key answer tips
This question, about a group of two companies, is split into two unrelated areas.
Part (a) requires you to calculate the corporation tax liability for each of the companies. There
are capital and trading losses to deal with.
Part (b) has two requirements: firstly, to explain the reporting of real time PAYE information
to HM Revenue & Customs (‘HMRC’); and secondly to state which forms must be provided to
employees or submitted to HMRC following the end of the tax year. The highlighted words
in the answer to part (b) below are key phrases that markers are looking for.
Tutor’s top tips
It is easy to overrun on part (a), so you could consider answering part (b) before part (a) to
make sure that you do not run out of time to answer both parts of the question.
(a) Corporation tax computations
Tutor’s top tips
When you read the information, you see that one company has a capital loss and one has a
trading loss. The requirement states that reliefs must be claimed as soon as possible so you
will need to consider how relief can be taken for these losses.
You were told the amount of premium taxed on the landlord as income, not the premium
itself, so all that is needed to calculate the tax allowable amount is to divide this figure by the
number of years in the lease.

the lease premium taxed on the landlord as property income can be deducted from

title: Q270 · MAXIMUM LTD
scenario:
This scenario relates to two requirements.
The following information is available in respect of Maximum Ltd for the year ended
31 March 2026:
Trading profit
The trading profit based on the draft accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026 is £127,200.
This figure is before making any adjustments required for:
(1) A premium which was paid on 1 August 2025 to acquire a leasehold office building on
an eight-year lease. The amount of premium assessed on the landlord as income was
£22,320. The office building was used for business purposes by Maximum Ltd
throughout the period 1 August 2025 to 31 March 2026.
(2) Leasing costs of £10,300 which have been deducted in arriving at the profit of
£127,200. The leasing costs relate to two cars which have been leased since 1 April
2025. The first car has CO2 emissions of 40 grams per kilometre and is leased at an
annual cost of £6,400. The second car has CO2 emissions of 120 grams per kilometre
and is leased at an annual cost of £3,900.
(3) Employee bonuses of £36,000, which have not been deducted in arriving at the profit
of £127,200, all of which relate to the year ended 31 March 2026. Maximum Ltd paid
£20,000 of the bonuses on 30 November 2026, with the remainder of £16,000 paid on
15 February 2027. No entitlement to the bonuses arose until the time that they were
paid.
Property business income
Maximum Ltd lets out a freehold warehouse which is surplus to requirements. The building
was let from 1 April to 31 October 2025 but, although it was available for letting, it was empty
from 1 November 2025 to 31 January 2026. Because it was not possible to find new tenants,
the warehouse was sold on 31 January 2026 (see chargeable gains).
The following income and expenditure was incurred during the period 1 April 2025 to
31 January 2026:
Date received/(paid)  |  £
1 January 2025  |  Rent for the six months ended 30 June 2025  |  8,400
1 April 2025  |  Insurance for the year ended 31 March 2026  |  (1,320)
1 July 2025  |  Rent for the four months ended 31 October 2025  |  5,600
31 October 2025  |  Repaid security deposit of one month’s rent  |  (1,400)
20 January 2026  |  Advertising for tenants  |  (720)
31 January 2026  |  Insurance refund (less an administrative fee)  |  190
Chargeable gains
Maximum Ltd made two disposals during the year ended 31 March 2026:
(1) On 31 January 2026, Maximum Ltd disposed of a freehold warehouse (see property
business income) for £187,000. The disposal resulted in a chargeable gain of £43,300.
The warehouse was never used by Maximum Ltd for business purposes.
(2) On 20 February 2026, Maximum Ltd disposed of a freehold factory for £142,000. The
disposal resulted in a chargeable gain of £29,100. The factory was used by Maximum
Ltd for business purposes.
On 10 December 2025, Maximum Ltd had purchased a new factory for £342,000. This factory
is used for business purposes. Maximum Ltd made the maximum possible rollover relief claim
against the new factory cost of £342,000.
No rollover relief claim has been, or will be, made in respect of the premium paid for the
eight-year lease (trading profit note (1)).
Donations
During the year ended 31 March 2026, Maximum Ltd made qualifying charitable donations
of £2,800 and political donations of £700. Neither of these amounts have been deducted in
arriving at the trading profit figure of £127,200.
Subsidiary companies
Maximum Ltd has two subsidiary companies, both of which commenced trading on 1 April
2023. Each company made a trading profit for the year ended 31 March 2026. The following
information is available:
Subsidiary  |  Percentage shareholding  |  Trading profit
Xim Ltd  |  85%  |  £21,400
Mum Ltd  |  65%  |  £13,800
Neither company has any other income or outgoings, with neither making a trading profit for
the year ended 31 March 2025.
Brought forward losses
Maximum Ltd has the following brought forward amounts of unused losses from the year
ended 31 March 2025:
£
Trading loss  |  (288,200)
Property business loss  |  (3,800)
Capital loss  |  (4,900)
requirement:
Required:
(a) Before taking account of brought forward losses, apart from any losses which are
automatically relieved, calculate Maximum Ltd’s taxable total profits for the year
ended 31 March 2026. 
Note: Your computation should commence with the trading profit based on the draft
accounts figure of £127,200, indicating by the use of zero (0) any items that do not
require adjustment.   (11 marks)
(b) On the basis that the maximum possible loss relief and group relief claims are made
for the year ended 31 March 2026, calculate the total remaining amount of unused
losses which Maximum Ltd can carry forward to the year ended 31 March 2027.
Note: If possible, your loss relief claims should not result in donations becoming
unrelieved.   (4 marks)
(Total: 15 marks)

MAXIMUM LTD
Key answer tips
Part (a) tests you on your adjustments to profit knowledge. There are three adjustments to
deal with here. You also need to calculate property income and chargeable gains where there
is rollover relief to consider for one of the disposals. Make sure you answer the question set
(to calculate TTP) as it could be tempting to continue and calculate the CT liability which is
not asked for here.
Part (b) looks at loss relief and group relief. Be careful here with the percentage holdings in
the various companies.

The capital loss b/f is automatically offset against the first available capital gains and is

Examiner’s report
The corporation tax question was fairly well answered, although many candidates had
difficulty when it came to requirement (b).
Along with a trading profit, for the year ended 31 March 2026 Maximum Ltd had property
business income and chargeable gains. The company made qualifying charitable donations
and political donations during the year. Maximum Ltd had brought forward amounts of
trading loss, property business loss and capital loss.
Maximum Ltd had two subsidiary companies. Xim Ltd was a 75% group company, whereas
Mum Ltd (with a 65% shareholding) was not.
Requirement (a)
One important point to appreciate is that property business income and chargeable gains are
both included within the calculation of taxable total profits (TTP), yet a number of candidates
kept these elements entirely separate from the trading profit (even though all income and
gains form part of the TTP).
The starting point was to adjust the trading profit for three items:
Leasehold premium deduction (1.5 marks):  |  The essential point to appreciate here was that
the figure provided was the amount of premium assessed on the landlord (£22,320), and not
the amount of premium itself. Therefore, the first step in the calculation had already been
done. The relevant deduction was simply the assessed amount divided by the number of years
of the lease (8 years), with an 8/12ths restriction; the lease being granted on 1 August 2025.
It was also important to realise that the final result (22,320/8 × 8/12 = £1,860) had to be
deducted in the main computation, not added.
Leasing costs disallowance (1.5 marks):  |  Leasing costs for two cars had been deducted in
arriving at the trading profit. The first car had CO2 emissions of 40 grams per kilometre, so no
adjustment was required. The second car had CO2 emissions in excess of 50 grams per
kilometre, so a 15% add-back was required. This adjustment often caused problems, with
various mistakes made. For example, sometimes the 15% add-back was applied for both cars,
or adjustment was made for the 85% deductible element of the leasing costs for the second
car.
Deduction for employee bonuses (1 mark):  |  Bonuses of £20,000 were paid on 30 November
2026, with a further £16,000 paid on 15 February 2027. No entitlement to the bonuses arose
until the time that they were paid. The essential point here is that only the bonuses paid
within nine months of the end of maximum Ltd’s period of account are deductible, so not
those paid on 15 February 2027.
Having calculated a revised trading profit figure, the next steps were to calculate the property
business income and chargeable gains:
Property business income (3 marks):  |  This was a fairly straightforward computation for
3 marks based around a freehold warehouse which was let for a seven-month period before
the warehouse was subsequently sold. There were many perfect answers. Some candidates
struggled with the insurance payment, often trying to restrict this to the period the
warehouse was let out or owned by Maximum Ltd. However, it should have been obvious
that this aspect was taken into account due to Maximum Ltd receiving a refund of the
insurance premium paid. The correct deduction was therefore simply the insurance premium
paid (£1,320) less the refund (£190).
Chargeable gains (3 marks):  |  The chargeable gains computation was somewhat more
complicated, although there were still a number of perfect answers. Some candidates did not
appreciate that they had been given the two relevant chargeable gain figures (a freehold
factory was sold as well as the freehold warehouse), so no chargeable gain calculations were
required. However, the gain on the disposal of the factory could be rolled over (the proceeds
being fully reinvested – and that is why proceed figures were provided). The gain on the
disposal of the warehouse could not be rolled over because this property was not used for
business purposes. It was also necessary to deduct the brought forward capital loss as this
was automatically relieved (however, the mark available was given even if this deduction was
made in the answer to requirement (b)).
Donations (1 mark): Finally, it was a matter of deducting the qualifying charitable donations,
and indicating (by the use of a zero) that no deduction was available for the political
donations; many candidates missed an easy half mark by not showing this zero, despite being
instructed to do so.
As already mentioned, with computations containing both additions and deductions,
candidates should be very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with
deductions shown clearly as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion.
It is best to avoid putting workings for two or three marks within the one cell, which is what
some candidates did with their business property income calculation. It is very easy to make
mistakes, and workings have to be clearly shown in order for marks to be awarded.
Requirement (b)
This requirement caused a lot of problems. Even if answering correctly, candidates often took
a very long-winded approach towards a final answer, wasting considerable time in the
process. Also, with what were often a half page of notes and workings, it was sometimes
difficult to find a candidate’s final answer.
As already mentioned, Maximum Ltd had brought forward amounts of trading loss
(£288,200) and property business loss (£3,800). The brought forward capital loss should have
been set against the chargeable gain, and is therefore irrelevant to this requirement.
Simply taking the brought forward trading loss and using this against the (candidate’s own
figure) taxable total profits of Maximum Ltd for the year ended 31 March 2026 scored
1.5 marks. Add in the brought forward property business loss, and that scored half the
available marks.
The other two marks were for dealing with the group relief aspects. One problem here,
however, was that some candidates got into considerable confusion by treating the trading
profits of the two subsidiary companies instead as trading losses. The correct treatment was
to offset the brought forward trading loss against the trading profit of Xim Ltd (£21,400), and
then to show or state that no relief was available against the profits of Mum Ltd. Many
candidates – despite correctly dealing with Xim Ltd – did not mention Mum Ltd.
Rather than an extensive set of workings, the entire 4-mark answer was therefore simply
£288,200 + £3,800 – own figure taxable total profits – £21,400 – £0.

title: Q271 · March/June 2024
requirement: Which TWO of the following taxpayers are most likely to benefit financially from voluntary registration for value added tax (VAT)?

options.text: A business which buys standard rated supplies and sells zero rated goods to members of the public
A business which buys zero rated supplies and sells standard rated goods to members of the public
A business which buys zero rated supplies and sells zero rated goods to members of the public
A business which buys standard rated supplies and sells standard rated goods to other VAT-registered businesses

full_worked_solution:
A and D
Voluntary registration is beneficial for traders who can recover their input VAT and either
make zero rated supplies (so will not have to charge higher prices inclusive of VAT), or make
supplies to other VAT registered businesses (who can recover the additional cost of the
output VAT charged).
A business which buys zero rated supplies and sells standard rated goods to members of the
public, will not benefit by voluntary registration since it will not recover VAT on its purchases
(as these have no VAT being zero rated) and will have to charge members of the public an
extra 20% to recover the VAT on sales.
A business which buys zero rated supplies and sells zero rated goods to members of the
public will not benefit from voluntary registration as there is no VAT to be charged on sales
or recovered on expenses.

title: Q274 · VAT: outline
scenario: Betty, a retailer, decides to voluntarily register for VAT.
requirement: Which TWO of the following statements, concerning supplies made to Betty before the date of VAT registration, are TRUE?

options.text: Betty CAN reclaim input VAT on a car that she purchased six months ago, which she still uses for both private and business purposes
Betty CANNOT reclaim input VAT on the petrol used in her car, for both private and business purposes, in the month prior to the date of VAT registration
Betty CAN reclaim input VAT on a van purchased for the business two years ago which she still uses in the business
Betty CAN reclaim input VAT on accountancy services she purchased one year ago in connection with setting up the business
Betty CAN reclaim input VAT on the cost of goods bought for resale two months ago, which she sold the week before registration

full_worked_solution:
B and C
VAT cannot be reclaimed on cars which are used for private purposes.
VAT can normally be reclaimed on fuel used partially for private purposes (although output
VAT will be due based on the fuel scale rate). However, the fuel has been consumed prior to
the date of registration and therefore the input tax cannot be reclaimed.
Input tax can only be reclaimed on goods and assets if they are still on hand (or not
consumed) at the date of registration and they were purchased within four years prior to
registration.
Pre-registration input VAT can only be reclaimed on services if they were supplied within six
months of registration.
Pre-registration input VAT can be reclaimed on goods acquired for the business provided they
are on hand (i.e. in inventory) at the date of registration.

scenario:
Marina is a UK VAT registered trader making only standard-rated supplies. She purchased
goods worth £10,000 (VAT-exclusive) from a trader situated in Narnia. The goods would be
classed as standard-rated if they were supplied in the UK. The standard rate in Narnia is 5%.
requirement: What is the net effect on the VAT position of the UK trader?

options.text: £2,000 to pay to HM Revenue & Customs
£2,000 to reclaim from HM Revenue & Customs
£500 to pay to HM Revenue & Customs

full_worked_solution:
A
Marina accounts for output VAT of £2,000 as the goods would be standard-rated if supplied
in the UK. She can claim back input VAT of £2,000 on the same return as the goods are used
by a trader that only makes taxable supplies. The net effect on VAT payable is therefore nil.
Tutorial note
The rate of VAT in the overseas country is irrelevant. You should always use the rate of VAT
in the UK for calculations.

title: Q292 · VAT: outline
requirement: September 2020 OT question In which of the following cases must an appeal be made directly to the Tribunal?

options.text: A company appealing against a penalty for late filing of a corporation tax return
A company appealing against a penalty for late filing of employer year end returns
An individual appealing against a penalty for late registration for value added tax (VAT)
An individual appealing against a penalty for late payment of capital gains tax

full_worked_solution:
C
Examiner’s report
The correct answer is C, because appeals relating to indirect taxes must be made directly to
the Tribunal. Many candidates selected A, which is not correct because for direct taxes,
appeals must first be made to HMRC.
This is a challenging question on tax administration, an area which candidates often appear
to struggle with. Candidates are reminded of the importance of being prepared for questions
on all aspects of the syllabus, including tax administration, which is an important aspect of
TX-UK.

title: Q294 · CANDY APPLE AND SUGAR PLUM (ADAPTED)
scenario:
Answer debrief
Candy Apple
Candy Apple began a trading business on 1 April 2025. Her sales since the start of trade have
been as follows:
April to July 2025  |  £11,200 per month
August to November 2025  |  £15,100 per month
December 2025 to March 2026  |  £22,200 per month
These figures are stated exclusive of value added tax (VAT). Candy’s sales are all standard-
rated and arise evenly over the month.
As her accountant you have advised Candy in writing that she should be registered for VAT,
but she has refused to register because she thinks her net profit is insufficient to cover the
additional cost which would be incurred.
Sugar Plum
Sugar Plum began trading on 1 April 2025 and registered for VAT on 1 May 2025 to avoid late
registration penalties. The following information is available in respect of Sugar Plum’s VAT
for the quarter ended 31 July 2025:
1  |  Invoices were issued for standard-rated and zero-rated sales of £53,700 and £23,100
respectively. These figures are exclusive of VAT.
2  |  Sugar uses a room at her home as her office. The house has seven main rooms. The
VAT charged on the electricity bill for the whole house for the quarter is estimated as
£49.
During the quarter, Sugar also purchased several items of furniture for her office for a
total of £1,500 exclusive of VAT. A 5% discount was applied to this amount as Sugar
had purchased two items or more.
3  |  Prior to starting business, Sugar engaged a consultancy firm to undertake some market
research. Sugar paid the consultancy firm £250 on 1 August 2024 and £375 on
1 January 2025. Sugar also purchased £2,500 worth of inventory on 1 January 2025, of
which £1,000 was unsold by 1 May 2025. These figures are exclusive of VAT.
requirement: Answer all 5 linked Objective Test questions (2 marks each = 10 marks total).

options.prompt:
From what date was Candy Apple compulsorily required to charge VAT on her
taxable supplies and by what date must she notify HM revenue & Customs that she
is required to register for VAT?
Charge VAT from
1 November 2025  |  1 December 2025
31 October 2025  |  A  |  B
Notify
30 November 2025  |  C  |  D
options.worked_solution:
D
Candy was liable to compulsory register for VAT when her taxable supplies during any
12-month period exceeded £90,000.
This happened on 31 October 2025 when taxable supplies amounted to £90,100
(£11,200 + £11,200 + £11,200 + £11,200 + £15,100 + £15,100 + £15,100).
Candy was required to notify HMRC within 30 days of the end of the month in which
the threshold was exceeded (i.e. 30 November 2025) and was registered, and required
to charge VAT on taxable supplies, from the first day of the second month after her
taxable supplies exceeded the threshold (i.e. from 1 December 2025).

title: Q297 · THE WHITLOCK SISTERS (ADAPTED)
scenario:
Sisters Beth and Amy Whitlock trade as a partnership.
1  |  The partnership has been registered for VAT for many years and on 1 January 2026 it
began using the flat rate scheme to calculate the amount of VAT payable. The relevant
flat rate scheme percentage for the partnership’s trade is 13%.
2  |  For the quarter ended 31 March 2026 the partnership had standard-rated sales of
£50,000 and exempt sales of £10,000. For the same period standard-rated expenses
amounted to £27,300. The input VAT in relation to the expenses is all recoverable. All
figures are stated inclusive of VAT.
3  |  The partnership has two private rooms in its premises that can be hired by customers.
Such customers can book the rooms up to two months in advance, at which time they
have to pay a 25% deposit.
An invoice is then given to the customer on the day after the room hire, with payment
of the balance of 75% required within seven days. For VAT purposes, the renting out
of the rooms is a standard-rated supply of services.
4  |  Beth and Amy are planning to make significant changes to the partnership’s accounts
payable and accounts receivable processes and plan to take key suppliers and clients
out for dinner to explain the changes. The VAT-inclusive cost of this in the quarter to
30 June 2026 will be as follows:
UK customers  |  £250
UK suppliers  |  £100
Overseas customers  |  £775
Overseas suppliers  |  £650
requirement: Answer all 5 linked Objective Test questions (2 marks each = 10 marks total).

options.prompt: How much VAT is payable by the partnership for the quarter ended 31 March 2026 if the flat rate scheme is used?
options.worked_solution:
D
Using the flat rate scheme to calculate its VAT liability the partnership will have paid
VAT of £7,800 (£50,000 + £10,000) × 13% for the quarter.
Tutorial note
Under the flat rate scheme, VAT is calculated by applying a fixed percentage to the turnover
figure inclusive of VAT and including any exempt or zero-rated supplies. Expenses and
purchases are not relevant.

options.prompt:
How much VAT would be payable by the partnership for the quarter ended 31 March
2026 if the flat rate scheme was NOT used?
options.worked_solution:
£3,783
If the partnership had used the normal basis it would have paid VAT of £3,783
((£50,000 – £27,300) = £22,700 × 20/120).

1  |  Calculate the VAT element of VAT-inclusive prices using either 1/6 or 20/120 of the VAT-
inclusive price.
2  |  Output tax is not charged on exempt supplies.

options.prompt: Select the actual tax point date for the 25% deposit and 75% balancing payment in respect of the room hire.
options.worked_solution:

When the deposit is paid  |  Invoice date
The basic tax point date (BTP) is the date when the service is completed, which will be
the date that the room is used, i.e. the day of the room hire.
In respect of the 25% deposit the BTP is overridden by a payment before the BTP and
that payment date becomes the actual tax point.
In respect of the 75% balancing payment the BTP is not overridden by either a payment
or an invoice being issued before the BTP. However, as the invoice is issued within
14 days of the BTP, the invoice date becomes the actual tax point.
Tutorial note
For services, the basic tax point (BTP) is the date the service is provided/completed.
The actual tax point (ATP) can be either before or after the BTP.
The ATP will be before the BTP if:
•  |  An invoice is issued before the BTP, or
•  |  A payment is received before the BTP (as in this case with the deposit payments).
The ATP will be after the BTP if:
•  |  An invoice is issued within 14 days of the BTP, or
•  |  The business has an agreement with HMRC for a different date (typically businesses
agree a month end invoicing policy so that the invoice date is usually the ATP).

D

Input VAT incurred on business entertaining cannot be recovered, with the exceptions of staff

title: Q299 · ARDENT (ADAPTED)
scenario:
Ardent Ltd was incorporated on 1 April 2025 and started trading on 1 January 2026. The
company voluntarily registered for valued added tax (VAT) on 1 January 2026, preparing its
first VAT return for the quarter ended 31 March 2026. Ardent Ltd’s sales have been as
follows:
Standard-rated  |  Zero-rated
£  |  £
2026 January  |  24,800  |  30,100
February  |  42,600  |  28,700
March  |  58,300  |  22,700
–––––––  |  –––––––
125,700  |  81,500
–––––––  |  –––––––
Where applicable, the above figures are stated exclusive of VAT.
During the period 1 April to 31 December 2025, Ardent Ltd incurred input VAT of £120 each
month in respect of payments made for advertising services. The company also incurred
input VAT totalling £400 (£200 each) in respect of the purchase of two laptop computers on
10 July 2025. One of the laptop computers was scrapped on 30 November 2025 at a nil value,
and the other laptop was not used until Ardent Ltd started trading on 1 January 2026.
During the quarter ended 31 March 2026, Ardent Ltd received standard-rated invoices
totalling £56,400 (inclusive of VAT) in respect of purchases and expenses. As at 31 March
2026, £11,400 (inclusive of VAT) of the purchases was unsold and therefore included in
inventory.
Ardent Ltd was late in submitting its VAT return for the quarter ended 31 March 2026. The
company currently does not use either the VAT cash accounting scheme or the annual
accounting scheme.
requirement: Answer all 5 linked Objective Test questions (2 marks each = 10 marks total).

options.prompt: For each of the following statements concerning Making Tax Digital (MTD) select whether it is true or false:

rows: MTD software is used to print out returns which can then be sent to HMRC
The usual VAT return and payment submission dates apply
Although returns are produced automatically, the business is still responsible for checking them
The rules apply to all VAT registered businesses, including those with taxable supplies below the VAT registration threshold

Tutorial note
From 1 April 2025 all VAT registered businesses are required to use MTD, whether or not their

provided the services were supplied for business purposes. The input VAT incurred on

provided the goods are acquired no more than four years prior to registration and the goods
are still held at the date of registration. This rule applies equally to capital items as well as
current assets such as inventory and consumables.

The VAT incurred from the point of registration is recoverable regardless of whether the goods

title: Q300 · DENZIL DYER (ADAPTED)
scenario:
Denzil Dyer has been a self-employed printer since 2014. He has recently registered for value
added tax (VAT).
Denzil’s sales consist of printed leaflets, some of which are standard-rated and some of which
are zero-rated. He sells to both VAT registered customers and to non-VAT registered
customers.
Denzil offers a discount of 5% to those customers that pay within one month of the date of
the sales invoice. A customer, Tracey, placed an order for £500 of goods (exclusive of VAT)
and Tracey paid within one month of the date of the sales invoice.
All of Denzil’s printing supplies are purchased from a VAT registered supplier, Paper Ltd. He
pays by credit card and receives a VAT invoice. In the year ended 31 March 2026, Denzil
purchased some printing supplies from Paper Ltd for £800 (inclusive of VAT). Denzil also
purchases some office supplies by cash from various other suppliers for £200 (inclusive of
VAT), without receiving any invoices. All of these purchases are standard-rated.
Denzil does not use the annual accounting scheme, the cash accounting scheme or the flat
rate scheme.
requirement: Answer all 5 linked Objective Test questions (2 marks each = 10 marks total).

options.prompt: For each of the following statements, select whether it is true or false in relation to standard-rated and zero-rated supplies:

rows: Output VAT is only due in respect of standard-rated supplies.

Incorrectly classifying a supply as zero-rated would not remove Denzil’s liability to pay the output VAT which is calculated on the actual price charged. This would then be an additional cost to the business.
The type of supply, whether standard-rated or zero-rated, has no effect on the recovery of input VAT for Denzil.

Tutorial note
Prompt payment discounts are applied (if the customer qualifies for them) before calculating
the VAT payable. As the price is exclusive of VAT, the VAT is calculated at 20%. The amount
paid by Tracey will include the VAT.

options.prompt: Select TWO of the following conditions, which must be met in order for Denzil to recover input VAT on purchases.

options.text: The supply must be made to Denzil since he is the taxable person making the claim for input VAT
The supply must be supported by evidence, normally in the form of a VAT invoice
Denzil must only pay for all of his purchases by credit card
Denzil can recover all input VAT paid on purchases which are partly for private and partly for business purposes

options.worked_solution:
A and B
Tutorial note
Denzil can recover input VAT on purchases paid for in cash as long as he receives a VAT invoice.
Denzil must use the goods or  |  services supplied for business purposes, although an
apportionment can be made where supplies are acquired partly for business purposes and
partly for private purposes (except in the case of the purchase of a car).

options.prompt:

supplies and office supplies in the year ended 31 March 2026?
options.worked_solution:
£133
Printing supplies: £800 × 1/6 = £133 input VAT.
Tutorial note
The supply must be supported by evidence, normally in the form of a VAT invoice. Denzil will
therefore not be able to recover any input VAT in respect of the purchases of office supplies
for cash, where there is no invoice.

options.prompt: Select TWO of the following statements which are correct in relation to Denzil issuing VAT invoices to customers.

options.text: Denzil must issue a VAT invoice when he makes a zero-rated supply to one of his VAT registered customers
A simplified invoice can be issued if the supply is less than £250
A VAT invoice is required to be issued for a standard-rated supply to a non-VAT registered customer
A VAT invoice should be issued within 30 days of the date that the supply of the services is treated as being made

options.worked_solution:
B and D
Tutorial note
Denzil must issue a VAT invoice when he makes a standard-rated supply to one of his VAT
registered customers. A VAT invoice is not required if the supply is zero-rated or the supply is
to a non-VAT registered customer (e.g. a member of the public) – then an invoice need not be
issued unless the customer requests.

title: Q301 · KRISTEL
scenario:
Kristel commenced trading as a retailer of ladies and children’s clothes on 1 July 2024. She
registered for value added tax (VAT) on 1 August 2025, and is currently completing her VAT
return for the quarter ended 31 October 2025. All of the amounts stated below are exclusive
of VAT.
Sales of clothing
Kristel's quarterly sales were:
£
Ladies’ clothes (standard rated)  |  7,200
Children’s clothes (zero rated)  |  1,600
Kristel offered a prompt payment discount on sales made during August 2025. The amount
of discount taken was £230 of which £140 related to sales of ladies’ clothes and £90 related
to sales of children’s clothes.
Car and marketing services
On 16 September 2025, Kristel purchased a new car for £8,000. She uses the car 40% for
business purposes.
On 1 October 2025, Kristel paid £220 for marketing services to a company situated overseas.
Inventory for own use
During the quarter ended 31 October 2025, Kristel took ladies clothes from inventory for
herself. These had a replacement value of £90 but had a selling price of £125.
requirement: Answer all 5 linked Objective Test questions (2 marks each = 10 marks total).

options.prompt: What is the amount of output VAT which Kristel will have to include on her VAT return for the quarter ended 31 October 2025 in respect of her sales of clothing?
options.worked_solution:
D
£

Output VAT on zero-rated sales ((£1,600 – £90) × 0%)  |  0
–––––

–––––

options.prompt: What amount of input VAT will Kristel be able to reclaim in respect of the purchase of the car and the marketing services paid during the quarter ended 31 October 2025?
options.worked_solution:
B
£
Input VAT on marketing services (£220 × 20%)  |  44
Input VAT on car  |  0
–––––
Total input VAT  |  44
–––––
Tutorial note
Input VAT is reclaimable on marketing services only. The same amount would be accounted
for as output VAT under the reverse charge procedure, since the marketing services were
supplied by a company situated overseas, however the question only asks for the input VAT
figure.
No VAT can be reclaimed in respect of the car since it is used partly for private purposes.

options.prompt: What additional amount of output VAT will Kristel have to include on her VAT return for the quarter ended 31 October 2025 in respect of the clothes which she took from inventory for her own use?
options.worked_solution:
B
£90 × 20% = £18
Tutorial note
Where goods are removed from a business for personal purposes, a taxable supply arises and
the value of that supply of goods for VAT purposes is the replacement value.

options.prompt:
Kristel is able to issue simplified (or less detailed) VAT invoices to some of her
customers.
Which of the following does NOT need to be shown on such a simplified invoice?

options.text: A description of the goods supplied
The total amount of VAT charged

options.worked_solution:
D
Tutorial note
A less detailed VAT invoice does not need to show the total amount of VAT charged. The other
items must appear on a simplified invoice.

discount).
Sales for the quarter ended 31 January 2026 were:

Total sales of children's clothes (zero rated)  |  6,300
These figures are stated exclusive of VAT.
No discounts were offered.

Tutorial note
Under the flat rate scheme, the VAT payable is calculated by applying the flat rate percentage
to the total taxable supplies of the business.

title: Q302 · LIAN
scenario:
You should assume that today’s date is 20 February 2026.
Lian is registered for value added tax (VAT), but does not use any of the special VAT schemes.
All of her supplies are standard rated for VAT.
Lian has just completed her VAT return for the quarter ended 31 December 2025.
Office equipment
On 28 September 2025, Lian signed a contract to purchase standard rated office equipment.
On that date, she paid a deposit of £2,400.
The equipment was delivered on 23 December 2025, but, because of the New Year holiday,
an invoice for the balance of the purchase price of £7,200 was not raised until 3 January 2026.
Lian paid the balance of the purchase price on 17 January 2026.
Both of the above figures are exclusive of VAT.
Impairment losses
On 31 December 2025, Lian wrote off three impairment losses:
Invoice date  |  Payment date due  |  Output VAT originally paid
18 May 2025  |  18 June 2025  |  £420
21 June 2025  |  21 July 2025  |  £360
3 August 2025  |  3 September 2025  |  £100
Submission of VAT returns
Because of the busy New Year period, Lian was late in submitting her VAT return for the
quarter ended 31 December 2025 and in paying the related VAT liability of £19,400. The
return was submitted and payment was made on 20 February 2026.
Similarly, Lian was late in submitting her VAT returns and in paying the related VAT liabilities
for the quarters ended 31 December 2022, 31 June 2024 and 31 December 2024. All of her
other VAT returns have been submitted on time and the related VAT liabilities paid on time.
Services acquired from overseas
During the quarter ended 31 March 2026, Lian will purchase specialist engineering services
from a VAT registered overseas supplier at a cost of £4,000. This figure is exclusive of VAT.
The rate of VAT in the supplier's country is 15%.
requirement: Answer all 5 linked Objective Test questions (2 marks each = 10 marks total).

options.prompt: How much input VAT should Lian have claimed on her VAT return for the quarter ended 31 December 2025 in respect of the office equipment?
options.worked_solution:
D
The payment of the deposit on 28 September would have been included in the
quarterly return to 30 September 2025.
The delivery of the equipment on 23 December 2025 is the basic tax point but because
the invoice was raised within 14 days of this, the invoice date becomes the actual tax
point, being 3 January 2026. This will be reported in the quarterly return to 31 March
2026 and not in the return to December 2025.

options.prompt: What amount of input VAT should Lian have included on her VAT return for the quarter ended 31 December 2025 in respect of the three impairment losses?
options.worked_solution:
B
Since the claim for the impairment loss is made more than six months after the due
date for payment of 18 June 2025, this output VAT can be reclaimed. The payment due
dates for the other two invoices are not outstanding for more than six months as at
31 December 2025.

options.prompt:
What penalties (if any) will Lian have to pay in respect of the late submission of her
VAT return and late payment of VAT for the quarter ended 31 December 2025?
Penalty for late submission
£0  |  £200
£0  |  A  |  B
Penalty for late
payment
£582  |  C  |  D
options.worked_solution:
A
The penalty point in respect of the first late submission for the quarter ended
31 December 2022 will have expired after two years (i.e. by 31 December 2024) as at
that point the threshold of four points had not been reached. The late submissions for
the quarters ended 31 June 2024 and 31 December 2024 each incur a penalty point.
Therefore, the late submission for the quarter ended 31 December 2025 incurs the
third penalty point and there will not yet be a financial penalty.
No penalty for late payment is charged if VAT is paid within 15 days of the due date.
The payment was due on 7 February 2026 and made on 20 February 2026, therefore
no penalty is payable.

options.prompt: If Lian were to use the annual accounting scheme, with a VAT annual return period ending on 30 June, which VAT advantage could she benefit from?
options.worked_solution:
B
Since only one VAT return is submitted each year under the annual accounting scheme
the reduced administration means that penalties could be avoided in respect of late
submissions. Lian would also have an extra month to submit her return which would
also help with this.
Tutorial note

title: Q303 · MABEL
scenario:
You should assume today’s date is 20 March 2026.
Mabel, a sole trader, is registered for value added tax (VAT) and is in the process of
completing her VAT return for the quarter ended 28 February 2026. Mabel does not use the
VAT cash accounting scheme.
Outputs
During the quarter ended 28 February 2026, standard rated sales invoices totalling £98,000
(exclusive of VAT) were issued in respect of credit sales. Mabel offers all of her customers a

customers paid within the 14-day period.
Inputs
During the quarter ended 28 February 2026, standard rated purchase and expense invoices

20% related to private calls). All of these figures are inclusive of VAT.
Cessation
Mabel wishes to retire and is therefore going to cease trading on 31 March 2026. She will
deregister for VAT. Mabel is unsure whether she will sell the assets of her business separately
to different purchasers after ceasing to trade, or whether she will sell the entire business as
a going concern on 31 March 2026. During the previous three years, Mabel has purchased

November 2025 for £350
2  |  A car purchased (for both business and private use) during August 2025 for £9,600

All of the non-current asset figures are exclusive of VAT.

title: Q304 · SILVERSTONE LTD (ADAPTED)
scenario:
This scenario relates to three requirements.
Silverstone Ltd is registered for value added tax (VAT), but currently does not use any of the
special VAT schemes. The company has annual standard-rated sales of £1,200,000 and
annual standard-rated expenses of £550,000. Both these figures are exclusive of VAT and are
likely to remain the same for the foreseeable future.
Silverstone Ltd is up to date with all of its tax returns, including those for corporation tax,
PAYE and VAT. It is also up to date with its corporation tax, PAYE and VAT payments. The
company has never had a conviction for any VAT offences. However, the company often
incurs considerable overtime costs due to its employees working late in order to meet tax
return filing deadlines.
Silverstone Ltd pays its expenses on a cash basis, but allows customers two months credit
when paying for sales. The company does not have any impairment losses.
Silverstone Ltd is planning to purchase some new machinery at a cost of £22,000 (exclusive
of VAT). The machinery will be purchased from an overseas supplier. Silverstone Ltd is not a
regular importer and so is unsure of the VAT treatment for this purchase.
Silverstone Ltd is also planning to start selling goods overseas for the first time and wants to
understand how the sales with be treated for VAT purposes. All of these sales will be
standard-rated.
requirement:
Required:
(a) Explain why Silverstone Ltd is entitled to use both the VAT cash accounting scheme
and the VAT annual accounting scheme, and why it will probably be beneficial for
the company to use both schemes.  (6 marks)
(b) Explain when and how Silverstone Ltd will have to account for VAT in respect of
the: 
1  |  purchase of machinery, and
2  |  overseas sales.   (4 marks)
(Total: 10 marks)
